newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Costa Rica's Picado bids for U.N. human rights job.
newsitem.headline: Costa Rica's Picado bids for U.N. human rights job.

text.p: Sonia Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to Washington, on Thursday spoke to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan about becoming the new U.N. commissioner for human rights.
"I was there for an interview," Picado told reporters. "He (Annan) is very open about seeing different candidates. There are many regions. He is going to take his time."
Her main opponent for the job is President Mary Robinson of Ireland whose government has nominated her for the job when she ends her presidency at the end of the year.
But it is doubtful the post would remaind vacant until then and diplomats said it was unclear if Robinson would leave Ireland before she completes her term.

Picado, the choice of Latin American and Caribbean states, stressed women's rights and education as key components of the job. In a nod to the Third World she also ranked economic and social rights on the same level as political and civil rights.

The post, first suggested nearly 50 years ago, became vacant after Jose Ayala Lasso resigned last month as the first U.N. high commissioner for human rights to become Ecuador's foreign minister. He was appointed in 1994 for a four-year term.

Latin American delegates argue that at minimum a candidate from their region should be appointed to complete Ayala Lasso's term. Numerous developing nations agree, contending that the West has more than its share of senior U.N. jobs.

Picado is an author, the first woman judge in her country and the first woman in Latin America to be elected dean of a law school. She has received U.N. awards for rights work and has served on the Inter-America court of human rights.
Annan is known to prefer a woman in the post, which has to be approved by the 185-member General Assembly.

Also mentioned is Finland's former defence minister Elizabeth Rehn, now the U.N. investigator for human rights in the ex-Yugoslavia. But her chances are considered slim compared to those of Robinson and Picado.
Ayala Lasso, whose Geneva-based office is short of funds and understaffed, had been criticised for his low-profile in not publicly condemning more rights abuses.
In answer to queries, Picado said she was not going to analyse Ayala Lasso's work, saying only the commissioner should speak out strongly on issues and also negotiate, depending on the case.
"My work with women has been done throughout my whole career. Woman rights are human rights -- and that has not been true in the world," she said.

"You have to educate and change mentalities in the world, with our children, with the military and with the state in general," she said, adding: "You cannot just address civil and political rights and civil liberites. You have to work with economic and cultural rights."
